title: Google releases Gemini 4 Neon, a cheaper tier that tops the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index
subtitle: The new middle-tier model slots between Carbon and Hydrogen, runs at $3 input and $15 output per million tokens with a 1M-token context, and ships to AI Studio and the Gemini app on Pro and Ultra.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Neon on the evening of November 18, 2026, positioned between the top-end Gemini 4 Carbon and the fast Hydrogen tier launched earlier this month. Pricing is $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output, with a 1 million token context window. Rollout covers the Gemini API in Google AI Studio, Gemini for Business, and the Gemini app for Pro and Ultra subscribers. Google's announcement claims Neon tops the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index and is 32% cheaper per task than Carbon, and MarkTechPost reports a score of 61 on the broader AA Intelligence Index — third overall.

The pricing is the news. Neon undercuts Opus 5.5 at roughly the same coding-agent capability per vendor-reported benchmarks, and it does so with a 1M-token window that keeps long-running agentic tasks in a single call rather than forcing chunking. For buyers running agent swarms — code review, refactoring, security triage — the per-task economics flip in Google's favor at this price point. Carbon still leads on hard reasoning, but Carbon rarely wins on the long-horizon coding workloads that drive production spend.

This is Google's third frontier release of November, after Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 14 and the Genie 4 world-model public release earlier in the month. The cadence matters because Google is now shipping tier-by-tier rather than one annual flagship, which gives enterprise buyers price-anchored options at each capability level. For comparison, Anthropic ships roughly twice a year and OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on November 18. The three labs are converging on a three-tier model-release pattern: a top reasoning model, a mid-tier price-performance model, and a fast low-cost tier.

For learners: the benchmark claims in launch posts are vendor-reported and almost never match third-party evaluation. The useful signal is price per task on a workload you actually run. Build a small eval set of 20 to 30 representative prompts, run it on Neon, Carbon, and Opus 5.5 through the API, and compare. The gap between marketing number and your number tells you whether the headline benchmark is a signal about the model or a signal about the test.
